## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Abbhantarajātaka* (Ja 281), translated as "The Midmost Mango", is a narrative included in the *Jātaka* section of the Pali Khuddaka Nikāya [SuttaCentral]. The commentary records that the story was told by the Buddha while residing at Jetavana, occasioned by the Elder Sāriputta offering mango juice (*ambarasadāna*) to the nun Bimbādevī (the mother of Rāhula) [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879]. In the commentary's narrative background, Rāhula's mother, reflecting that both her husband and her son had embraced the religious life, decided to move to Sāvatthī and become a monastic so she could continuously be in their presence [Ratanamalai 2007]. In the story of the past, the text opens with the verse line *Abbhantaram nāma dumo ti* ("There grows a tree") [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879]. Notably, the Jātaka portrays Sakka in a pre-Buddhistic disposition plotting to destroy a group of ascetics, rather than acting in his typical role as a guardian of virtue [Adikaram 1946].

SuttaCentral lists four modern translations of the text in four languages and identifies no external parallels [SuttaCentral]. Computational text-reuse analysis via DharmaNexus confirms internal reuse exclusively with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (three matching passages, the longest being §1.2–2.4 corresponding to §2553–2557 with a similarity score of 0.94), while finding no cross-language matches meeting the detection threshold [DharmaNexus].
